title: Given two sequences, find the length of the longest subsequence common to both, preserving order but not requiring contiguity. Explain the two-dimensional dynamic programming, the row-rolling optimisation, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Longest Common Subsequence (Longest Order-Preserving Match Between Two Sequences)

s1_definition.profdef: The Longest Common Subsequence finds the longest sequence of elements appearing in both inputs in the same relative order, not necessarily contiguously. A grid cell holds the best length for the two prefixes: when the current characters match it is one plus the diagonal cell, otherwise it is the better of dropping one character from either side. The grid reduces to two rolling rows.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India compares two versions of a transaction log for the same account and wants the longest ordered set of matching entries, which reveals the shared backbone and highlights what was inserted or removed.
s1_definition.oneliner: On a match add one to the diagonal, otherwise take the better of the two neighbours.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Longest Common Subsequence finds the longest sequence of elements appearing in both inputs in the same relative order, not necessarily contiguously. A grid cell holds the best length for the two prefixes: when the current characters match it is one plus the diagonal cell, otherwise it is the better of dropping one character from either side. The grid reduces to two rolling rows.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India compares two versions of a transaction log for the same account and wants the longest ordered set of matching entries, which reveals the shared backbone and highlights what was inserted or removed.

**One line to remember:** On a match add one to the diagonal, otherwise take the better of the two neighbours.

sections.s2_technical:
We build a grid where the cell at row i and column j is the length of the longest common subsequence of the first i elements of the first sequence and the first j elements of the second. If the i-th and j-th elements are equal, the cell is one plus the diagonal cell above-left, because we extend the match. If they differ, the cell is the larger of the cell above, which drops the i-th element, and the cell to the left, which drops the j-th element. The bottom-right cell is the answer.

The fill core is `for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) dp[i][j] = a.charAt(i-1) == b.charAt(j-1) ? dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 : Math.max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]);`. A concrete check: for ABCBDAB and BDCAB the longest common subsequence has length four, for example BCAB. Senior nuance: the time is the product of the two lengths and the space can drop from that product to twice the shorter length by keeping only the previous and current rows; reconstructing the actual subsequence requires either the full grid or stored direction choices.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India keeps two versions of a transaction log for the same account, one from the core banking system and one from a reconciliation feed, and wants the longest ordered sequence of matching entries to identify the shared backbone and spot inserted or dropped entries. Comparing entry by entry misses matches that are out of alignment. This is exactly how Longest Common Subsequence works: it finds the longest order-preserving match.

The code defines a `LogComparisonService` with `longestCommonLength(logA, logB)` using the row-rolling grid. A `Demo` provides two logs and logs the common-length.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is two log versions, ABCBDAB and BDCAB. Step 1: we keep a previous row and a current row of length six, all zeros, representing the empty-prefix base case. Step 2: processing the first version's A against the second version, no match extends anything meaningful yet. Step 3: as we process B, matches with the second version's B set cells to one plus their diagonal. Step 4: processing C, B, D, A, B in turn, each match extends the diagonal and each mismatch copies the better neighbour, so the lengths climb along aligned matches. Step 5: after the last row is filled and rolled, the final cell holds four. Step 6: we return four as the longest common backbone length, corresponding to a shared ordered set such as BCAB.

    Post: length of longest common subsequence

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Longest Common Subsequence finds the longest ordered set of elements that appears in both inputs without requiring them to be contiguous, and it is the backbone of diff tools and version comparison. I model it as a grid where the cell at row i, column j is the best common length between the first i elements of one sequence and the first j elements of the other. The recurrence has just two cases: if the current two elements match, the cell is one plus the diagonal cell, because the match extends the previous solution; if they differ, the cell is the larger of the cell directly above and the cell directly to the left, each of which drops one element from one side.

The optimisation I always mention is that each cell depends only on the current and previous rows, so I keep two rolling rows and reduce the space from the full product of the two lengths down to the length of the shorter sequence. If I also need the actual common subsequence rather than just its length, I either retain the full grid or store the direction choice at each cell and walk backward from the bottom-right corner.

At the National Bank of India I used this to compare two versions of an account's transaction log, one from the core system and one from a reconciliation feed, to extract the longest ordered set of matching entries and thereby highlight what had been inserted or dropped. I ran the rolling-row version so memory stayed small even on long logs. Explaining the match-extends-the-diagonal rule, the drop-one-side rule for mismatches, and the row-rolling space optimisation is what shows an interviewer I understand this foundational two-sequence dynamic programming.
